title: Charles Darwin
description: An illustrated map of the life of Charles Darwin, from Shrewsbury and Cambridge around the world on HMS Beagle, by Brazil, Patagonia, the Andes and the Galápagos, to Down House in Kent, where he worked out evolution by natural selection and published On the Origin of Species.
mapLabel: Illustrated world map following the life of Charles Darwin and the voyage of the Beagle, 1809 to 1882
note: Based on Darwin's own Journal of Researches, notebooks, letters and autobiography, and on later biographies. The Beagle's route is simplified to its main stops. Places in England sit closer together than a pin on this world map, so routes between them are not drawn. The map is stylised and not to scale.

steps.title: A doctor's son in Shrewsbury
steps.text: Charles Robert Darwin was born at The Mount in Shrewsbury on 12 February 1809, the son of a wealthy doctor, Robert Darwin. His grandfathers were the physician Erasmus Darwin and the potter Josiah Wedgwood. His mother died when he was eight. At Shrewsbury School he preferred collecting shells, minerals and beetles to Latin and Greek.
steps.today: Today: The Mount still stands, and his statue sits outside Shrewsbury Library, once his school.

steps.title: Medicine in Edinburgh
steps.text: His father sent him to study medicine at Edinburgh. He found the lectures dull and fled two operations performed without anaesthetic. He learned to stuff birds from John Edmonstone, a freed man from Guiana who had been enslaved, and explored sea creatures on the shore with the zoologist Robert Grant, an early believer in evolution.
steps.today: Today: The University of Edinburgh has named a building after him.

steps.title: Beetles at Cambridge
steps.text: Next his father sent him to Christ's College, Cambridge, to become a country clergyman. He took his degree but spent his passion on collecting beetles. The botanist John Stevens Henslow became his mentor, and in 1831 Henslow recommended him as a gentleman naturalist for a surveying voyage around the world on HMS Beagle.
steps.today: Today: His rooms at Christ's College are restored, and a statue of him as a student stands in the college garden.

steps.title: The Beagle sails
steps.text: His father at first refused, but his uncle Josiah Wedgwood II changed his mind. The Beagle's captain, Robert FitzRoy, was 26 and wanted a gentleman companion for a long survey of the South American coast. After weeks of gales, the small ten-gun ship left Plymouth with 74 people aboard. Darwin was terribly seasick.
steps.today: Today: The voyage was meant to last two years. It lasted almost five.

steps.title: Seashells in a cliff
steps.text: At St Jago in the Cape Verde Islands, he saw a white band of seashells running through a cliff high above the sea. He had brought the first volume of Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology, which argued that the Earth changes slowly through forces still at work. The band suggested the land had risen.
steps.today: Today: St Jago is Santiago, the main island of Cape Verde.

steps.title: Rainforest and slavery
steps.text: In Brazil he walked into tropical rainforest for the first time and wrote that he was in a state of delight. He also saw slavery. When FitzRoy defended it, Darwin's angry reply almost cost him his place on the ship. He stayed months around Rio de Janeiro, collecting insects, spiders and plants.
steps.today: Today: Bahia is Salvador, Brazil, which abolished slavery only in 1888.

steps.title: Giants in the gravel
steps.text: Near Bahía Blanca in Argentina, he dug the bones of huge extinct mammals out of low cliffs: a giant ground sloth (Megatherium) and the hippo-sized Toxodon. They resembled smaller animals still living in South America. Why should extinct and living creatures in the same land be so alike? The question stayed with him.
steps.today: Today: Some of his Punta Alta fossils are in the Natural History Museum in London.

steps.title: Tierra del Fuego
steps.text: FitzRoy was returning three Fuegians whom he had taken to England on an earlier voyage, among them Orundellico, called Jemmy Button. Darwin was shocked by the Fuegians he met and described them harshly. The mission FitzRoy left behind collapsed within weeks. The Beagle spent many months surveying these channels and the Falkland Islands.
steps.today: Today: The Beagle Channel, named on the ship's first voyage, divides Argentina and Chile.

steps.title: An earthquake in Chile
steps.text: Darwin was resting in a forest near Valdivia when a great earthquake struck. At Concepción he found the city in ruins. FitzRoy measured shellfish beds raised above the tide line at nearby Santa María Island: the land had risen by about two to three metres in a moment. Darwin saw Lyell's slow changes at work.
steps.today: Today: Concepción, rebuilt after several earthquakes, is one of Chile's largest cities.

steps.title: Across the Andes
steps.text: He crossed the Andes on horseback by the Portillo pass to Mendoza and returned by another. High in the mountains he found fossil seashells, and a forest of petrified trees that had once grown by the sea. Mountains, he concluded, had been raised over immense time by many movements like the earthquake he had felt.
steps.today: Today: The movement of the Earth's plates explains how seabeds were lifted into the Andes.

steps.title: The Galápagos Islands
steps.text: In five weeks on these volcanic islands, he collected birds, plants and reptiles. The vice-governor said he could tell which island a giant tortoise came from by its shell. Darwin noticed mockingbirds differed between islands. He did not label most of his finches by island; their importance became clear only back in London.
steps.today: Today: The islands are a national park of Ecuador, and the finches are called Darwin's finches.

steps.title: Across the Pacific
steps.text: The Beagle crossed the Pacific by Tahiti and New Zealand to Sydney. Riding inland over the Blue Mountains, he watched a platypus and wondered at Australia's strange animals. In his diary he imagined an unbeliever saying that two distinct creators must have been at work. He did not much like the colony and was homesick.
steps.today: Today: The Charles Darwin Walk at Wentworth Falls follows part of his route in the Blue Mountains.

steps.title: How coral atolls form
steps.text: At the Cocos (Keeling) Islands he studied a coral atoll, a ring of reef around a lagoon. He had already guessed how such rings form: corals grow upward around a volcanic island while it slowly sinks, until only the reef is left. It was his first major theory and made his name among geologists.
steps.today: Today: Drilling on Enewetak atoll in 1952 found volcanic rock beneath the coral, as he had predicted.

steps.title: A visit to Herschel
steps.text: At the Cape of Good Hope he met the astronomer John Herschel, who was mapping the southern sky. Herschel had called the appearance of new species the mystery of mysteries, and hoped it would be explained by natural causes. Darwin later said meeting him was one of the most memorable events of the voyage.
steps.today: Today: An obelisk in Claremont, Cape Town, marks where Herschel's telescope stood.

steps.title: Home to England
steps.text: The Beagle went by St Helena and Ascension, crossed again to Bahia, and finally reached Falmouth after almost five years. Darwin rode straight to Shrewsbury. His letters and specimens, sent home through Henslow, had already made him known to scientists. He never left Britain again, and was often unwell for the rest of his life.
steps.today: Today: The Beagle ended as a coastguard watch ship and was broken up; her remains may lie in Essex mud.

steps.title: A tree of life
steps.text: In London the ornithologist John Gould told him his Galápagos birds included a group of distinct finch species, and three kinds of mockingbird. Species, Darwin began to think, were not fixed. In July 1837 he drew a branching tree in a private notebook and wrote above it, “I think.” He told almost no one.
steps.today: Today: The notebook is in Cambridge University Library; missing for years, it was returned anonymously in 2022.

steps.title: Malthus and marriage
steps.text: In September 1838 he read Thomas Malthus on population: more are born than can survive. Darwin saw that in the struggle, small helpful variations would be kept and harmful ones lost. He called it natural selection. He also drew up a list headed “Marry” and “Not marry,” and in January 1839 married his cousin Emma Wedgwood.
steps.today: Today: University College London's Darwin Building stands where their first home on Gower Street was.

steps.title: Down House
steps.text: Seeking quiet for his health and family, they moved to Down House in Kent. In 1844 he wrote a 230-page essay on his theory and left Emma a letter asking her to publish it if he died. Then he spent eight years on barnacles, partly to earn the authority to write about species.
steps.today: Today: Down House is a museum, and his thinking path, the Sandwalk, is open to visitors.

steps.title: Annie
steps.text: His beloved eldest daughter, Annie, fell ill, and he took her to Malvern for the water cure, which he had tried himself. She died there aged ten, probably of tuberculosis. Darwin wrote a private memoir of her. Her death is often said to have ended what was left of his Christian faith.
steps.today: Today: Annie's grave is in the Priory churchyard at Great Malvern.

steps.title: A letter from Ternate
steps.text: In June 1858 a letter reached Down from Alfred Russel Wallace, a collector in the Malay Archipelago. It set out almost the same theory of natural selection. Darwin was stunned: “all my originality... will be smashed.” Wallace dated it from Ternate, though he may have written it on nearby Halmahera, as historians debate.
steps.today: Today: Ternate is an island in North Maluku, Indonesia, still ringed by clove plantations.

steps.title: On the Origin of Species
steps.text: His friends Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged for both men's papers to be read at the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Neither author was there; Darwin's baby son had just died. Darwin then wrote what he called an abstract. On the Origin of Species appeared on 24 November 1859 and sold out to booksellers.
steps.today: Today: The Linnean Society still meets at Burlington House on Piccadilly.

steps.title: The Oxford debate
steps.text: At a meeting of the British Association in Oxford, Bishop Samuel Wilberforce attacked the theory, and Thomas Henry Huxley defended it. Wilberforce is said to have asked Huxley whether he descended from an ape on his grandmother's or grandfather's side. Accounts of the exchange differ. Darwin, unwell, stayed home and followed it by letter.
steps.today: Today: The Oxford University Museum of Natural History, where the debate took place, still stands.

steps.title: Orchids, emotions and worms
steps.text: From Down he wrote book after book: on orchids, on variation under domestication, on climbing and insect-eating plants. The Descent of Man (1871) applied his theory to humans and added sexual selection. He studied facial expressions in people and animals. His last book, in 1881, showed how earthworms slowly turn and build the soil.
steps.today: Today: A worm stone like the one he used to measure the burying work of worms sits in the garden at Down House.

steps.title: Westminster Abbey
steps.text: Darwin died at Down House on 19 April 1882, aged 73. His family planned a village burial, but scientists and members of parliament pressed for a national funeral. He was buried in Westminster Abbey. Evolution by natural selection, backed since by genetics and fossils, became the foundation of modern biology.
steps.today: Today: His grave in Westminster Abbey lies a few feet from Isaac Newton's.

items.name: Robert FitzRoy
items.text: A naval officer and aristocrat who captained the Beagle at 26. Brilliant at surveying and quick-tempered, he and Darwin shared a cabin for five years and quarrelled over slavery. A devout Christian, he later opposed Darwin's theory. He became governor of New Zealand and founded the Met Office, issuing the first public weather forecasts.

items.name: John Stevens Henslow
items.text: Professor of botany at Cambridge, a clergyman and a generous teacher. Darwin was known as “the man who walks with Henslow”. Henslow recommended him for the Beagle, received the specimens he sent home and shared his letters with scientists, so Darwin was already known when he returned. Henslow later accepted some of his pupil's theory.

items.name: Emma Darwin
items.text: Emma Wedgwood, his first cousin, married Darwin in 1839. They had ten children, three of whom died young. A sincere Christian, she worried that his views would part them in the afterlife, and told him so, yet supported his work, read his manuscripts and nursed him through decades of illness.

items.name: Charles Lyell
items.text: The Scottish geologist whose Principles of Geology argued that the Earth was shaped slowly by forces still acting. Darwin read it on the Beagle and saw its ideas at work. Lyell became his friend and urged him to publish before he was forestalled, and arranged the 1858 reading with Hooker. He accepted evolution only slowly.

items.name: Joseph Hooker
items.text: A botanist and traveller who later directed Kew Gardens. In 1844 Darwin wrote to him that believing species could change was “like confessing a murder.” Hooker became the closest friend of his working life, read drafts, sent plants and data, and with Lyell arranged the joint reading of Darwin's and Wallace's papers in 1858.

items.name: Alfred Russel Wallace
items.text: A self-taught naturalist who paid his way by selling specimens from the Amazon and the Malay Archipelago. He reached natural selection independently and sent his essay to Darwin in 1858. He accepted the joint publication graciously and called his own book on the subject Darwinism. He later mapped the line between Asian and Australian animals.

items.name: Thomas Henry Huxley
items.text: A largely self-taught biologist who became evolution's fiercest public defender, called “Darwin's bulldog”. He argued against Bishop Wilberforce at Oxford in 1860 and showed how closely human anatomy resembled that of apes. He was never fully convinced that natural selection was the main cause of evolution. He coined the word agnostic.

items.name: Orundellico (Jemmy Button)
items.text: A Yaghan boy taken to England by FitzRoy in 1830, renamed Jemmy Button, and taught English and English manners. He returned on the Beagle in 1833 and soon went back to his own people's way of life, telling FitzRoy he had no wish to return to England. His story is a sharp chapter of colonial history.
